INTERVENOR AARON EDWARD HOWTON'S EXCEPTIONS TO THE
PROPOSAL FOR DECISION AND MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT
Filed September 1, 2026
TO THE HONORABLE COMMISSIONERS OF THE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS:
Pursuant to 16 Texas Administrative Code (TAC) § 22.261 and the Commission Counsel's Exceptions and Replies Memorandum, Intervenor Aaron Edward Howton, appearing pro se as Party No. 250, timely files these Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision (PFD) issued August 20, 2026. The PFD is PUC Interchange Item No. 6441. The filing deadline for exceptions is September 2, 2026. (Exceptions and Replies Memorandum, PUC Interchange Item No. 6442.)
I. SUMMARY AND LIMITED SCOPE OF THESE EXCEPTIONS
Mr. Howton agrees with and asks the Commission to adopt the PFD's principal recommendation: deny the Bell County East-to-Big Hill and Big Hill-to-Sand Lake CCN applications. The PFD correctly concludes that the record does not establish that the requested CCN amendments are necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public and that the applications should also be denied because approximately 1,400 later-affected landowners were deprived of the public-meeting process required by 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4). (PFD at 38-46, 84-99, 159-62, 194-96; Findings of Fact 22-30 and 120-48; Conclusions of Law 10-15; Proposed Ordering Paragraph 2.)
These exceptions are limited to the PFD's conditional routing determination. Mr. Howton excepts to Section VIII.A.1 and the related discussion in Sections VIII.B through VIII.L, to Findings of Fact 155, 160, 167-68, 169, 176, 180, 194-95, 197-205, 213, 222-23, and 244, and to Conclusion of Law 16, only to the extent those provisions find that Route 894 is the best route if the Commission approves the project. Route 894 includes Link F20. (PFD at 103, 147-48, 183-95.)
Mr. Howton's first and controlling request is denial of the project. If the Commission does not deny the applications, Mr. Howton requests selection of Route 296, not Route 894. Route 296 avoids Link F20 and, on this record, better protects environmental integrity, uses existing compatible corridors more effectively, and avoids the uncorrected F20 defects described below. At an absolute minimum, the Commission should reject Link F20 and select a record-supported non-F20 route.
II. AUTHORITIES AND PRINCIPAL RECORD REFERENCES
A. Statutes and Rules
1. PURA § 37.056(a), (c), including community values, recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, and cost.
2. 16 TAC § 25.101(a)(3), (a)(6), and (b)(3)(B), including habitable structures, prudent avoidance, compatible rights-of-way, property lines, and moderation of impacts to landowners and communities.
3. 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4), public-meeting notice and participation requirements for transmission-line CCN applications.
4. 16 TAC § 22.261, proposals for decision, exceptions, replies, and Commission action.
B. Principal Record Materials
1. Proposal for Decision, PUC Interchange Item No. 6441 (Aug. 20, 2026) (PFD).
2. Aaron Edward Howton Initial Post-Hearing Brief, PUC Interchange Item No. 6257 (June 19, 2026) (Howton Initial Brief).
3. Hearing on the Merits Transcript, Volumes 1-6, PUC Interchange Item No. 6137 (June 8-12, 2026) (Tr.).
4. Aaron Edward Howton Direct Testimony and Exhibits, including environmental, tornado, agricultural, cultural-resource, route-map, and prudent-avoidance evidence, PUC Interchange Item No. 3988.
5. Notice of Cultural Resource Within 1,000 Feet of Link F20 Centerline, PUC Interchange Item No. 5925; First Cedar Valley Baptist Church Direct Testimony, PUC Interchange Item No. 3995.
6. Applicants' Application and Environmental Assessment, App. Ex. 1; Applicants' Errata, App. Ex. 1A; Applicants' Combined Data Table, App. Ex. 23; and admitted Howton exhibits cited below.
III. EXCEPTIONS FOLLOWING THE PFD OUTLINE
VIII.A.1. Route 894 (Central Corridor)
Mr. Howton excepts to the premise that Route 894 can be selected from the existing data as the best route. The PFD states that Route 894 was Applicants' preferred route and recognizes that Mr. Howton supported Route 296. (PFD at 103, 105.) But identifying an Applicant-preferred route does not establish that the underlying route data are accurate. Route 894 includes F20, and the F20-specific record contains admitted omissions affecting habitable structures, a church and community gathering place, cultural and archaeological resources, water features, threatened- and endangered-species habitat, and disaster-recovery conditions.
The demonstrated omissions matter because the PFD's conditional recommendation rests heavily on comparative tables. A route comparison cannot be reliable when a material link on the chosen route was evaluated through desktop, GIS, aerial, flyover, and drive-by methods without adequate site-specific ground verification. Applicants' witness did not personally walk F20 or obtain the local information needed to resolve the identified constraints before recommending Route 894. (Tr. Vol. 2 at 117:1-124:8; Howton Initial Brief at 8-12; PUC Interchange Item No. 6257.)
VIII.B. Intervenor Concerns Regarding Routing Methodology
The PFD itself recognizes that Applicants did not assign weights to routing factors, did not run a sensitivity analysis, and produced a process criticized as a non-reproducible 'black box.' It also acknowledges testimony that different weighting choices can produce different route selections and that another qualified reviewer could reasonably reach a different conclusion. (PFD at 107-08, citing 4K Land Exs. 1 and 5; Tr. Vol. 3 at 57-59; Tr. Vol. 4 at 87.)
Once record evidence established concrete errors on F20, the PFD should not have treated the uncorrected EA tables as conclusive. No rule necessarily requires Applicants to retain an independent third party for every data point, but PURA § 37.056(c)(4) does require a reliable comparison of the statutory factors. The proper remedy is denial, as the PFD recommends. If the Commission nevertheless chooses a route, it should not select the route whose disputed link was not adequately verified and corrected.
VIII.C. Community Values
The PFD defines community values as a shared appreciation of an area or mutual resource and recognizes that adverse effects include significant changes to the use, enjoyment, or intrinsic value of a community resource. (PFD at 109, citing Docket Nos. 41606 and 44060.) First Cedar Valley Baptist Church, established in 1942, is a longstanding worship center, meeting place, site of weddings and funerals, location for youth and senior events, and focal point for community support and tornado recovery. It lies approximately 690 to 720 feet from F20. Applicants did not include it in the F20 cultural-resource analysis because it was not on a Texas Historical Commission list. (Tr. Vol. 2 at 117:1-119:8; Howton Initial Brief at 10-11; PUC Interchange Item Nos. 5925 and 3995.)
The April 12, 2022 EF-3 tornado and the continuing Cedar Valley recovery are also community-value evidence. Applicants' EA did not identify that disaster, and the witness confirmed there was no specific routing criterion or guideline addressing a community recovering from a declared disaster. (Tr. Vol. 4 at 54:10-55:23; Howton Initial Brief at 12.) The lack of a separate disaster rule did not authorize the decision-maker to disregard the evidence; it should have been weighed under community values, aesthetic and historical values, environmental integrity, and moderation of landowner impacts.
Finally, the PFD correctly finds that approximately 1,400 newly affected landowners did not receive the public-meeting opportunity required by 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4). (PFD at 38-46; Findings of Fact 22-30; Conclusions of Law 10-15.) That prejudice is directly connected to F20: later-notified landowners had far less time to identify the omissions now shown in the record. The PFD cannot both recognize that prejudice as a basis for denial and, at the same time, treat the resulting F20 record as sufficiently reliable to select Route 894.
VIII.C.3. Future Development
The PFD states that proposed future development is not entitled to the same weight as existing constraints and that Commission precedent does not give significant weight to future plans unless development has been initiated in a readily observable or measurable way. (PFD at 115, citing Docket Nos. 45866, 55574, and 57648.) Applicants' witness described F20 as a post-public-meeting alternative developed in response to comments about planned development, yet did not identify a specific existing constraint that required the sharp turns through Cedar Valley and Buttermilk Creek. The witness acknowledged that more turning angles generally increase cost and that he did not walk the F20 area or speak with affected F20 landowners. (Tr. Vol. 2 at 120:18-124:8; Howton Initial Brief at 8-9.) To the extent speculative future development influenced F20, that choice is inconsistent with the precedent summarized by the PFD.
VIII.D. Recreational and Park Areas
The PFD states that Applicants defined parks and recreational areas to include areas owned by a governmental body or an organizational group, club, or church. (PFD at 116.) It then relies on the EA's statement that no park or recreational area lies within 1,000 feet of Route 894. (PFD at 116, 148; Finding of Fact 194.) The omitted church is within 1,000 feet of F20. At minimum, the Commission should require a corrected classification and a reasoned determination whether the church property and its recurring community activities fall within Applicants' own definition. The uncorrected zero cannot support a finding that Route 894 is superior.
VIII.E. Aesthetic and Historic Values
The PFD acknowledges that EA statistics do not capture every qualitative impact and that an area can have historical significance even if it has not been formally listed. (PFD at 120, 123.) Those principles apply directly to First Cedar Valley Baptist Church and the Buttermilk Creek drainage. Applicants did not field-survey the archaeologically sensitive F20 area before route selection, and the record identifies F20 as crossing land with high archaeological potential near the Buttermilk Creek/Gault cultural landscape. (Tr. Vol. 2 at 117:1-124:8; Howton Initial Brief at 11-13.)
Findings of Fact 198 through 201 treat the recorded-site counts as complete and conclude that Route 894 reasonably minimizes historical and archaeological impacts. That conclusion should be withdrawn or qualified because the route-specific evidence identified unrecorded community and cultural resources that the EA did not capture. A later construction-stop provision cannot restore a resource damaged by avoidable siting.
VIII.F. Environmental Integrity
The PFD's own comparative table shows that Route 894 crosses 0.09 mile of federally listed endangered- or threatened-species habitat, while Route 296 crosses 0.02 mile. Route 894 has the highest figure among the four Focus Routes. (PFD at 124.) The PFD also recognizes that Routes 296 and 392 perform favorably on environmental considerations because they use a Colorado River crossing with a pre-existing infrastructure corridor. (PFD at 147.)
F20-specific evidence further undermines the Route 894 conclusion. Applicants did not conduct a site-specific Golden-cheeked Warbler habitat survey before route selection and relied on GIS or agency mapping rather than ground verification. Mr. Howton's admitted evidence identified Tract 5645 as Golden-cheeked Warbler habitat and documented his observation and NRCS habitat review. (Tr. Vol. 4 at 52:23-54:8; Howton Direct Testimony and AEH Exhibits 11-14, PUC Interchange Item No. 3988; Howton Initial Brief at 11-12.)
Finding of Fact 244 proposes a field assessment of Route 894 only after route selection and before construction. (PFD at 193.) That sequence may support permitting and mitigation, but it cannot cure an unreliable pre-selection comparison. The Commission should not authorize F20 first and discover its decisive constraints later. If the evidence is insufficient to compare routes accurately now, the proper result is denial or limited remand, not conditional approval of Route 894.
VIII.I. Route Length and Use of Existing Compatible Rights-of-Way and Property Lines
Route 296 performs better than Route 894 on several corridor measures reported in the PFD. Route 296 parallels 11.8 miles of existing electric transmission lines compared with Route 894's 5.7 miles; 14.8 miles of public roads and highways compared with 4.5 miles; and 105.3 total miles of compatible rights-of-way compared with 98.0 miles. The corresponding percentages are 47.1% for Route 296 and 43.9% for Route 894. (PFD at 139.) The PFD also acknowledges that 'apparent' property boundaries are an imperfect and less reliable metric than actual infrastructure corridors. (PFD at 140-43.) These comparisons favor Route 296 and were not given adequate weight in the conditional selection of Route 894.
VIII.J. Prudent Avoidance
Prudent avoidance means limiting electric- and magnetic-field exposure that can be avoided with reasonable investments of money and effort. The PFD recognizes that routing away from places where people gather advances that policy and that habitable structures include churches and schools. (PFD at 143; 16 TAC § 25.101(a)(3), (a)(6).)
Applicants' F20 count omitted the Carl Simpson residence approximately 383 feet from the centerline. During cross-examination, the witness acknowledged that the residence appeared within 500 feet and that the count would be adjusted if the structure met Applicants' standard. (Tr. Vol. 4 at 51:8-52:21.) The corrected F20 comparison identifies at least three habitable structures within 500 feet, while F21 lists one. (Howton Initial Brief at 9-10.) The route-wide count of 85 for Route 894 therefore cannot be treated as an undisputed number.
The PFD also fails to account qualitatively for the church as a recurring gathering place merely because it lies beyond 500 feet. Prudent avoidance is a reasoned policy, not a rule that erases community gathering places at 501 feet. Because Route 894's F20 data understated both a residence and a longstanding gathering place, Findings of Fact 167 and 168 do not support the conclusion that Route 894 best achieves prudent avoidance.
VIII.K. Moderation of Impact to Landowners
Rule 25.101(b)(3)(B) requires reasonable moderation of impacts to affected communities and landowners. F20 would place the line approximately 100 feet from the boundary of Mr. Howton's Tract 5645 and approximately 240 feet from a residence, while burdening an active rural property used for cattle, wildlife management, family recreation, and residential purposes. (Applicants' Response to Howton RFI 1-05; Howton Initial Brief at 9.) The concentrated F20 burden, combined with late notice and the uncorrected resource omissions, is not a reasonable moderation of impact when a viable non-F20 route is available.
VIII.L. Routing Recommendation
The PFD acknowledges that Routes 296 and 894 have comparable length and cost, that cost is not a distinguishing factor, and that Route 296 performs favorably on environmental considerations by using a Colorado River crossing with a pre-existing infrastructure corridor. (PFD at 128-30, 147.) It nevertheless selects Route 894 principally because the EA reports fewer habitable structures and no park or recreational area within 1,000 feet. (PFD at 147-48.) Those are the very F20 data points shown to be incomplete.
Mr. Howton does not minimize the concerns about Florence Elementary School or the two churches identified on Route 296. The PFD notes that Florence Elementary School is approximately 395 feet from F34, that Applicants corrected its classification, and that a minor route adjustment may maximize distance from the school without changing other route-determining factors. (PFD at 109-11.) Those concerns should be addressed through the greatest lawful setback and careful final alignment. They do not justify selecting Route 894 on materially incomplete F20 data.
Accordingly, the Commission should retain the PFD's denial recommendation. If the Commission nevertheless approves a route, it should select Route 296 and require reasonable alignment adjustments to maximize distance from the Florence school and churches. Route 894 and Link F20 should be rejected.
IV. SPECIFIC EXCEPTIONS TO FINDINGS OF FACT AND CONCLUSION OF LAW
A. Findings of Fact 155 and 160
Exception: These findings recommend Route 894 and state that it appropriately balances routing factors. Requested revision: 'If the Commission does not deny the applications and selects a route, Route 296 provides the better record-supported balance of the routing factors. Route 894 and Link F20 should not be selected because the F20 data contain material, unresolved omissions affecting habitable structures, community values, cultural and historical resources, environmental integrity, and prudent avoidance.'
B. Findings of Fact 167-68
Exception: The finding that Route 894 has 85 known habitable structures is disputed by the admitted F20 omission, and the prudent-avoidance conclusion depends on that uncorrected count. Requested revision: 'Applicants' Route 894 count omitted at least one residence within 500 feet of F20 and did not adequately account for First Cedar Valley Baptist Church as a gathering place. The record does not establish that Route 894 best complies with prudent avoidance.'
C. Findings of Fact 169 and 176
Exception: The finding that community-value information was incorporated into route selection is incomplete as applied to F20. Requested revision: 'Route 894 does not adequately address the expressed Cedar Valley community values because the analysis omitted or inadequately weighed First Cedar Valley Baptist Church, the Buttermilk Creek cultural landscape, tornado recovery, agricultural and rural land use, and the prejudice caused by the lack of a public meeting for later-affected landowners.'
D. Findings of Fact 180 and 194-95
Exception: The PFD overstates Route 894's corridor and recreation-area advantages. Requested revision: 'Route 296 parallels more existing transmission-line and public-road infrastructure and a greater percentage of compatible rights-of-way than Route 894. The record does not support an unqualified finding that no park or recreational area lies within 1,000 feet of Route 894 until the omitted church property is evaluated under Applicants' own definition.'
E. Findings of Fact 197-205 and 213
Exception: The historical, archaeological, aesthetic, and environmental findings rely on uncorrected EA data. Requested revision: 'The Route 894 analysis did not adequately identify or weigh First Cedar Valley Baptist Church, the Buttermilk Creek archaeological and cultural concerns, F20 water features, or site-specific threatened- and endangered-species habitat. Route 894 crosses 0.09 mile of federally listed habitat compared with Route 296's 0.02 mile.'
F. Findings of Fact 222-23 and 244
Exception: Post-selection surveys and mitigation cannot supply the comparative information needed to select a route. Requested revision: 'The record does not establish that Route 894 best balances environmental integrity. Any field assessment needed to identify route-determinative water, cultural, migratory-bird, or threatened- and endangered-species constraints must occur before selection of Route 894, not merely after approval.'
G. Conclusion of Law 16
Exception: Conclusion of Law 16 conditionally selects Route 894. Requested replacement: 'If the Commission does not deny the applications, Route 296 provides the better balance of the routing considerations in PURA § 37.056(c)(4) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B), including environmental integrity, use of existing compatible rights-of-way, community values, historical and aesthetic values, prudent avoidance, and moderation of impacts to the affected community and landowners. Route 894 and Link F20 should not be approved.'
V. PRAYER
For these reasons, Aaron Edward Howton respectfully requests that the Commission: (1) adopt the PFD's recommendation denying the CCN applications; (2) sustain these exceptions to the PFD's conditional selection of Route 894; (3) reject Route 894 and Link F20; (4) if the Commission nevertheless approves the project, select Route 296 with reasonable final-alignment adjustments to maximize distance from the Florence school and churches; (5) alternatively, decline to select any route until material EA errors and omissions are corrected through an adequate, pre-selection field verification process; and (6) grant all other relief to which Mr. Howton may be entitled.
Respectfully submitted,

VIII.A.1. Route 894 (Central Corridor)
     Mr. Howton excepts to the premise that Route 894 can be selected from the existing data as
the best route. The PFD states that Route 894 was Applicants' preferred route and recognizes that

endangered-species habitat, and disaster-recovery conditions.
     The demonstrated omissions matter because the PFD's conditional recommendation rests
heavily on comparative tables. A route comparison cannot be reliable when a material link on the
chosen route was evaluated through desktop, GIS, aerial, flyover, and drive-by methods without
adequate site-specific ground verification. Applicants' witness did not personally walk F20 or

VIII.B. Intervenor Concerns Regarding Routing Methodology
     The PFD itself recognizes that Applicants did not assign weights to routing factors, did not
run a sensitivity analysis, and produced a process criticized as a non-reproducible 'black box.' It
also acknowledges testimony that different weighting choices can produce different route
selections and that another qualified reviewer could reasonably reach a different conclusion. (PFD
at 107-08, citing 4K Land Exs. 1 and 5; Tr. Vol. 3 at 57-59; Tr. Vol. 4 at 87.)
     Once record evidence established concrete errors on F20, the PFD should not have treated
the uncorrected EA tables as conclusive. No rule necessarily requires Applicants to retain an
independent third party for every data point, but PURA § 37.056(c)(4) does require a reliable
comparison of the statutory factors. The proper remedy is denial, as the PFD recommends. If the
Commission nevertheless chooses a route, it should not select the route whose disputed link was
not adequately verified and corrected.

VIII.C. Community Values
     The PFD defines community values as a shared appreciation of an area or mutual resource
and recognizes that adverse effects include significant changes to the use, enjoyment, or intrinsic
value of a community resource. (PFD at 109, citing Docket Nos. 41606 and 44060.) First Cedar
Valley Baptist Church, established in 1942, is a longstanding worship center, meeting place, site
of weddings and funerals, location for youth and senior events, and focal point for community
support and tornado recovery. It lies approximately 690 to 720 feet from F20. Applicants did not
include it in the F20 cultural-resource analysis because it was not on a Texas Historical
Commission list. (Tr. Vol. 2 at 117:1-119:8; Howton Initial Brief at 10-11; PUC Interchange Item
Nos. 5925 and 3995.)
      The April 12, 2022 EF-3 tornado and the continuing Cedar Valley recovery are also
community-value evidence. Applicants' EA did not identify that disaster, and the witness
confirmed there was no specific routing criterion or guideline addressing a community recovering
from a declared disaster. (Tr. Vol. 4 at 54:10-55:23; Howton Initial Brief at 12.) The lack of a
separate disaster rule did not authorize the decision-maker to disregard the evidence; it should have
been weighed under community values, aesthetic and historical values, environmental integrity,
and moderation of landowner impacts.
      Finally, the PFD correctly finds that approximately 1,400 newly affected landowners did not
receive the public-meeting opportunity required by 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4). (PFD at 38-46; Findings
of Fact 22-30; Conclusions of Law 10-15.) That prejudice is directly connected to F20: later-
notified landowners had far less time to identify the omissions now shown in the record. The PFD
cannot both recognize that prejudice as a basis for denial and, at the same time, treat the resulting
F20 record as sufficiently reliable to select Route 894.

VIII.J. Prudent Avoidance
     Prudent avoidance means limiting electric- and magnetic-field exposure that can be avoided
with reasonable investments of money and effort. The PFD recognizes that routing away from
places where people gather advances that policy and that habitable structures include churches and
schools. (PFD at 143; 16 TAC § 25.101(a)(3), (a)(6).)
     Applicants' F20 count omitted the Carl Simpson residence approximately 383 feet from the
centerline. During cross-examination, the witness acknowledged that the residence appeared
within 500 feet and that the count would be adjusted if the structure met Applicants' standard. (Tr.
Vol. 4 at 51:8-52:21.) The corrected F20 comparison identifies at least three habitable structures
within 500 feet, while F21 lists one. (Howton Initial Brief at 9-10.) The route-wide count of 85 for
Route 894 therefore cannot be treated as an undisputed number.

      The PFD also fails to account qualitatively for the church as a recurring gathering place
merely because it lies beyond 500 feet. Prudent avoidance is a reasoned policy, not a rule that
erases community gathering places at 501 feet. Because Route 894's F20 data understated both a
residence and a longstanding gathering place, Findings of Fact 167 and 168 do not support the
conclusion that Route 894 best achieves prudent avoidance.
